newsitem.title: USA: Conn Light puts regulatory assets near $1 bln.
newsitem.headline: Conn Light puts regulatory assets near $1 bln.

text.p: Connecticut Light and Power Co has almost $1 billion of regulatory assets on its books as a result of postponed collection of rate increases, chief financial officer John H. Forsgren told state legislators.

Forsgren, who has the same title at the utility's parent company, Northeast Utilities, told the legislature's Energy and Technology Committee CL&P has investment more than $2 billion in generating plants to serve the state and contracted to buy more than $270 million of power annually from indpendent power producers at costs exceeding the utility's cost to produce or purchase power.
"We expect that all these past prudent investments and commitments will be honored, in full, whether or not more competition is introduced into the electric industry," Forsgren said.

"Failure to do so ... could force a company or its investors into litigation, delay the path to competition and put Connecticut in a position out of step with mainstream pulic policymaking," he continued.
He suggested rates could be significantly lowered by refinincing these past commitments through rate reduction bonds, pointing out this would require legislative approval.
Commenting on proposed legislation, Forsgren recommended that Connecticut use laws passed by other states only as a springboard to devfining its own approach.
He said CL&P opposes some provisions in the draft law before the legislature, citing as especially troubling --
-- A proposal that only 75 percent of utility investment in generation be recoverable.
-- A proposal that extensive review by the Department of Public Utility Control be used to establish recoverable stranded costs.

These "time-consuming and expensive adminitrative proceedings...would delay the opportunity from customer savings from securitization, which we hope can occur as early as January 1998 and even may delay the January 2000 start-up of retail choice" suggested by the bill, he explained.
-- And, a suggested disallowance of Connecticut Yankee decommission costs would "quite clearly" conflict with federal law and regulatory practice.
